<section class="reviews-section">

    <div class="reviews-intro">
      <h1>Research Reviews</h1>
      <p class="page-subtitle">Planned critical analyses connecting key research to the AffineDrift framework</p>
      <div style="margin-bottom: 1.5rem; padding: 1rem 1.25rem; background: #f3f4f6; border-left: 4px solid #9ca3af; border-radius: 4px; font-size: 0.95rem; color: #4b5563;">
        <strong>Coming Soon.</strong> This section will contain detailed reviews connecting foundational
        biomechanics research to the drift/input decomposition framework. Reviews are planned but not yet written.
        The researcher profiles and paper lists below provide context on the work to be reviewed.
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="reviews-list">
      <article class="review-card">
        <div class="review-header">
          <h2>Interaction Forces in the Golf Swing</h2>
          <span class="review-date">Carol Putnam</span>
        </div>
        <div class="review-content">
          <p class="review-summary">
            Carol Putnam's work demonstrates how interaction forces between body segments automatically
            create the proximal-to-distal sequencing pattern in skilled golf swings. These forces
            facilitate energy transfer from larger, proximal segments to smaller, distal segments —
            a mechanism that maps directly onto the drift amplification concept in the AffineDrift
            framework.
          </p>
          <p style="font-style: italic; color: var(--text-light); font-size: 0.9rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">
            Review in progress. Key papers:
            Putnam (1993) "Sequential motions of body segments in striking and throwing skills,"
            <em>Journal of Biomechanics</em>, 26(S1), 125–135.
          </p>
        </div>
      </article>

      <article class="review-card">
        <div class="review-header">
          <h2>Induced Acceleration Analysis</h2>
          <span class="review-date">Felix Zajac &amp; Contributors</span>
        </div>
        <div class="review-content">
          <p class="review-summary">
            Felix Zajac's induced acceleration analysis decomposes segment accelerations into
            contributions from individual muscles and forces — the same causal attribution problem
            that the ZTCF addresses. Understanding how IAA handles intersegmental dynamics
            provides grounding for the AffineDrift drift/input decomposition.
          </p>
          <p style="font-style: italic; color: var(--text-light); font-size: 0.9rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">
            Review in progress. Key papers:
            Zajac &amp; Gordon (1989) "Determining muscle's force and action in multi-articular movement,"
            <em>Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews</em>, 17, 187–230.
          </p>
        </div>
      </article>

      <article class="review-card">
        <div class="review-header">
          <h2>Baseball Pitching Biomechanics</h2>
          <span class="review-date">Masahide Hirashima &amp; Contributors</span>
        </div>
        <div class="review-content">
          <p class="review-summary">
            Hirashima's work on baseball pitching biomechanics examines segment coordination, ground
            reaction forces, and energy transfer mechanisms in throwing. The cross-sport comparison
            with golf illuminates how sequential segment motion relates to the drift-amplification
            mechanisms in the AffineDrift framework.
          </p>
          <p style="font-style: italic; color: var(--text-light); font-size: 0.9rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">
            Review in progress. Key papers:
            Hirashima et al. (2008) "Kinetic chain of overarm throwing in terms of joint rotations,"
            <em>Medicine &amp; Science in Sports &amp; Exercise</em>, 40(4), 675–684.
          </p>
        </div>
      </article>

      <article class="review-card">
        <div class="review-header">
          <h2>Shaft Flexibility in Golf Swing Dynamics</h2>
          <span class="review-date">Sasho MacKenzie &amp; Contributors</span>
        </div>
        <div class="review-content">
          <p class="review-summary">
            Sasho MacKenzie's research on shaft flexibility examines how shaft stiffness, flex profile,
            and material properties influence swing mechanics and ball flight. This work is directly
            relevant to the elastic shaft modes in the ZTCF framework and the question of how
            shaft dynamics contribute to drift versus control.
          </p>
          <p style="font-style: italic; color: var(--text-light); font-size: 0.9rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">
            Review in progress. Key papers:
            MacKenzie &amp; Sprigings (2009) "A three-dimensional forward dynamics model of the golf swing,"
            <em>Sports Engineering</em>, 11(4), 165–175.
          </p>
        </div>
      </article>
    </div>

    <div style="margin-top: 3rem; padding: 1.5rem; background: var(--bg-secondary); border-radius: 8px; border: 1px solid var(--border-color);">

        <li><strong>Shaft Flexibility</strong> (MacKenzie) — elastic shaft modes and ZTCF validation</li>
        <li><strong>Baseball Pitching</strong> (Hirashima) — cross-sport comparison of sequential segment motion</li>
      </ol>
    </div>
